posts.title: A Pilgrim People
posts.description: There is just something about being at home, isn’t there? I am reminded of this every time I travel. When I wrote this column, it has been only a few weeks since we returned from a Ligonier study cruise in the Caribbean. We had a wonderful time of study and fellowship with Ligonier’s friends and supporters, many of whom are likely reading this column right now. Despite my enjoyment of the trip, however, I was happy to return home. I feel the same way every time I travel. I love my homeland and am happy to come back to the United States even after a blessed journey. Even though I am glad to come back to America, I must admit that when I come home to my country, I long to be elsewhere. At the end of the day, the United States is but an inn, a place to rest on the way to my true home—the city of heaven. As a Christian, I realize that I will never be truly home until I am with my Savior in heaven. The old spiritual puts it well: “This world is not my home . . . I’m just a passin’ through.”

posts.title: The Christian Virtue of Thanksgiving
posts.description: Gratitude is the heart’s response to grace, or at least it should be. Take Psalm 117, the shortest psalm in the Psalter and thereby the shortest chapter in Christian Scripture. It reads: “Praise the Lord, all nations! Extol him, all peoples! For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the Lord endures forever. Praise the Lord!” The psalmist cannot help but be overcome by gratitude and praise. And this is for a single reason only: God’s never-ending, covenant love which endures toward His people forever. Two elements of this petite psalm should jump right off the page at us. First is the scope of those who should be grateful. Does the psalmist believe that Israel alone should shout in acclamation? Is it limited to those who have Hebrew blood coursing through their veins? No. It is all the nations! All peoples! posts.title: The Importance of Prayers of Thanksgiving
posts.description: A phenomenon of recent years now attracts attention and gains steam each November: “secular Thanksgiving.” An article titled “Grateful Without God: A Secular Thanksgiving,” published several years ago, included interviews with people who insist on maintaining Thanksgiving as a holiday with significant meaning and purpose yet observe it as an entirely secular ritual. One person cited in the article sees Thanksgiving as an opportunity simply to “recognize that we are lucky in the grand scheme of the universe,” and others spoke of directing their thanks to friends or nature. The author noted the rising popularity of saying “secular grace” in gratitude before a meal. Several sample “secular grace” prayers and a link to a website with “Thanksgiving Non-Prayers for Humanists” concluded the article.
